analysis.one_liner: Makes permanent a tax deferral letting multinational corporations postpone US tax on certain foreign income.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced by Sen. Kyl in May 2007 with no cosponsors, sent to the Senate Finance Committee, and never received any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: US tax law generally taxes US companies on certain passive foreign income right away. This bill would make permanent an exception: when a US-owned foreign subsidiary pays dividends, interest, rents, or royalties to a related foreign company in the same corporate group, that income would not be taxed until brought back to the US. The exception was temporary and set to expire at the end of 2008; the bill removes that expiration date.
analysis.who_benefits: US-owned multinational corporations with chains of foreign subsidiaries, which could keep moving passive income (dividends, interest, rents, royalties) between related foreign companies without triggering immediate US tax, deferring payment indefinitely.
analysis.who_benefits_short: US multinational corporations with foreign subsidiaries

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the tax code to strike the 'before January 1, 2009' expiration, making the deferral exception permanent for payments between related foreign corporations.

Under the provision, dividends, interest, rents, and royalties received by a related entity from certain controlled foreign corporations are exempt from treatment as foreign holding company income, permitting tax deferral.

analysis.who_pays: US taxpayers generally, because deferred tax on offshore corporate income means revenue that would otherwise be collected now is postponed, possibly indefinitely.

drawbacks.text: Making the deferral permanent extends an exception that shields passive income held offshore from immediate US taxation, reducing revenue the government would otherwise collect.

The exception applied only to payments between related corporations in the same controlled group, so its main benefit flows to large multinational groups with sophisticated offshore structures rather than to ordinary businesses or households.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill had a narrow beneficiary set — multinational corporations with foreign subsidiaries — and its main effect was locking in a tax deferral that postpones US revenue. There were no provisions offsetting that cost or benefiting ordinary taxpayers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, and it died there when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Jon Kyl introduced the bill on May 2, 2007, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.
No cosponsors ever signed on to the bill.
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — was ever taken, and the bill expired with the 110th Congress on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: US taxpayers came out ahead, at least for the moment: the offshore tax deferral expired as scheduled at the end of 2008 instead of becoming permanent, though Congress has repeatedly extended similar provisions since.

for.name: Jon Kyl
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and spoke for it at introduction, but gathered no cosponsors.

against.name: Max Baucus
against.what_they_did: Committee to which the bill was referred; it never held a markup or vote on the bill, and it died there at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and there were no cosponsors, so there is no record of partisan support or opposition beyond the sponsor's party.

industries.industry: US multinational corporations with foreign subsidiaries
industries.note: The bill would have made permanent their ability to defer US tax on passive income passed between related foreign companies. Its cost falls on the general taxpayer in deferred revenue, so the industry's interest ran against the public's in this bill.
